title: USNH launches free tuition program for New Hampshire families making up to $100K - WMUR
content: A college education could soon be more affordable for some Granite State families. Starting next fall, the University System of New Hampshire will cover tuition for eligible in-state students from families making up to $100,000 per year. "We wanted to launch this program called the New Hampshire Promise to cover the cost of tuition for New Hampshire residents who make up to $100,000," said Kim DeRego, UNH vice provost for enrollment management. The New Hampshire Promise program applies to full-time first-year students and qualifying transfers at the University of New Hampshire, Plymouth State University and Keene State College. Some current students said the program sounds like a good idea. "That would be nice," said UNH senior Pacy Morgado. "I mean, I'm in-state, so, obviously, it's the highest in-state tuition in the country, so that would be helpful." "It's pretty exciting news," said UNH sophomore Brynna Kurspahic. "I've had a couple of friends that haven't been able to come back to school because they can't afford it anymore." The program will eventually replace a current one called the Granite Guarantee, and students will remain tuition-free for as long as they're eligible. A New Hampshire resident attending UNH can expect to pay $16,304 per year in tuition. Then, between housing, food and other fees, they have another $19,452 in costs. That adds up to more than $35,000 per year. Students in the program can get additional financial help in other ways. "Families can qualify for lots of other types of aid, including government aid and loans and things like that and other grant programs that are available," DeRego said. Some current students said they're worried about what the program could mean for their tuition, but university officials said there will be no impact. "We are not lowering the scholarships for students in order to fund these," DeRego said. "We're really trying to make the campus experience affordable for all of our students." Students don't need to apply for the program. They will be automatically considered when they fill out their FAFSA. title: A Conversation with Rosanna Warren - The New Hampshire
content: Rosanna Warren is a Connecticut-born poet, essayist, translator, biographer and former educator with a catalog of more than seven collections of poetry and literary criticism published throughout her esteemed career. Warren devoted as much time to her creative endeavours as she did teaching literature and the English language at numerous institutions, ranging from universities to Massachusetts medium-security prisons. A day before she read at the first of UNH’s Writer’s Series for the 26-27 academic year on Sept. 17, I was fortunate enough to be able to speak to Rosanna Warren for an exclusive interview. The following is a modified version of our conversation for brevity. It's an absolute pleasure to speak with you. How are you? That's a serious question these days, considering the country and the world. I take very seriously that we care about how we are. So I’m surviving. You’re reading at UNH tomorrow. As a deeply established poet, what compels you to do a reading today? It’s not advertisement. It's about sharing. It's about giving the work a life in the ear, in the eye, in the consciousness of potential audience, so it can have a life there. You started as a painter when you were attending Yale. Has being an experienced poet changed the way you engage with other art forms? I've been doing this for about 50 years. It’s all incremental and it's all come under the title of experience. I still do some drawing and listening to music, which is important to me and enters my experience of poems as well. I think the arts feed each other and live off each other in a good way. For instance, the music of Stravinsky and the music of Shostakovich matters to me in many ways, but partly because those are composers who push their art forward through forms of dissonance, which is what I'm trying to do in my poems. I come out of deep metrical traditions, and yet I'm also steeped in modernism and free verse. It’s about trying to marry those traditions of metrical order and dissonance. You put out a collection last year. Hindsight. How did that come together? What does it take for a collection to feel complete? That's a compositional question. In a sense, it just expands the attention one brings to an individual poem. What is the internal order and is it ever finished? It's about slowly groping one's way to a sense that a group may be coming together, cohering. In Hindsight, there are poems that were written during the COVID years, when my beloved and I lived in a very ramshackle shack up in the Catskill Mountains. Some of the poems were reflecting concerns—that's a mild way of putting it—and anguish at a country that was certainly in a very self-destructive state. So, part of the coherence of Hindsight is that not all the poems are overtly political—in fact, probably many of them you wouldn't think on the surface were political at all, but there's, underneath it, a deep political concern. What is the polis? What does it mean to be a citizen together? So that's part of the character of this book—mourning and anguish. But because some of these poems, many of them, were written when in a period of seclusion in the country, they're also full of nature. I grew up in the country, so I had always had a feel for animals and plants and the surround. But now with our ecological emergency, a planetary emergency, these poems that commune with nature, meditate on nature, have to me a more urgent character. It seems like Hindsight is a book largely about disconnect in a lot of ways. That's a really interesting comment. I accept that. And just to support it, the book ends with a poem called “Equinox,” which moves between the forest scene in the Catskills to a memory of the city, where the speaker of the poem remembers this figure who came out of the shadows of a hotel parking lot on a cold winter night. This young man was partly naked, and this encounter ends with disconnection. The last two lines of the poem, which are the last two lines of the book are “‘in our being, god is torn,’ said Simone Weil, ‘we walked away not in his world.’” That’s a powerful image. Is this path to understanding your world through poetry still a journey you find yourself on? Oh, yeah! I mean, I never even wanted to write poems. I wanted to be a painter, but writing eventually took over because I was writing all the time from childhood on. I simply cannot understand my life without poems. I do not understand things. So I need the poems. I need the struggle on the page to try to figure something out. That dissonance that you were referring to, has it evolved over time? Has it changed as to why you've written in that kind of form? Well, of course, because life changes. The world around you is changing. The world before 9-11 for Americans was different from the world after 9-11, just for one example. When The United States attacked Afghanistan and Iraq disastrously, I was trying to write poems that addressed the war, and I found that I could do it best obliquely. I did it through poems about Homer, poems about The Iliad. I did it through poems about Virgil, The Aeneid, the violence and birthing of the Roman Empire. So, my poems have been thinking about such matters for a long, long time, but in different ways and different languages. The cyclical quality of our species—how does that play into what you write about? Poetry is not journalism, nor is it an op-ed article. I didn't want my poems to sound like, “oh, I'm outraged we've attacked Iraq.” What we need is imagination. What poetry gives us is the deep imagination, of what is it to be at war? What is it to die? What is it to kill? And for that, I think we need Homer. We need The Odyssey. We need Gilgamesh. And then you make up your own list. But that's what culture is. It's finding imaginative and spiritual resources in order to interpret what's going on right now. Because it's really hard to interpret the present. It's really hard. It's blind man's bluff. It's very hard to see what's happening. You lived in both Italy and France, and have devoted a large chunk of your career to the art of translating. How did those experiences transform your art and your perception of art as a whole? It’s so enormous that I can't even measure it. I often told my students who wanted to be writers in English, “you need to start treating the English language like a foreign language.” You need detachment from it because you need to have more critical perspective on your own unconscious assumptions—about grammar, about vocabulary. A fundamental way to do that is you learn other languages. And by learning other languages, you're learning not just different words for things, you're learning different structures of reality. You're learning a whole different prosody. And that's important, to open your ear so you're not stuck unconsciously just reproducing whatever happens to be the pop song of the day, or the latest poem in the New Yorker or the APR. You need critical, artistic, aesthetic distance in order to create something real, I think. You have a book coming out in December, do you want to say anything about it? Yes, it's a family memoir. It's a book I resisted writing for many decades because my parents were well-known writers and I didn't want to be living off of their names. But they’ve been dead a long time and there were some stories I did want to tell about the life of writing. Their lives. So I had published a few individual essays about my mother's work and my father's work. And then they seemed to be tending toward being a book. What does your day-to-day work look like for you now? That's interesting. Part of it is homework and clerical, but serious in helping younger writers and scholars. This is the season when you write recommendations for grants. I think a lot about the person I'm writing for and what they've done and why I think they should get a grant or a job. That's not the main part of my work, but it's part of being a collective— to feel like we’re not alone, connected to one another. Since I'm not teaching anymore, I have a lot more time to sit in my chair that I call my poetry boat. I write by hand, and I write in my notebooks and muddle and struggle and try to make shapes come on the page. And sometimes they don't. Mostly they don't. Sometimes they do. And there's a lot of reading. It’s a sort of weaving of literary endeavors. Do you have any advice for the up-and-coming poets, who, quite possibly will be the defining poets of this generation? ‘Don’t let AI write your poems’ would be my main piece of advice. Don't get your brain invaded by capitalism to that extent. That's half serious…but actually, it is serious. Read…because I have met some younger poets who don't read very much, and I think that's a self-defeating, anti-artistic way to proceed. Don't just read your contemporaries and try to pick up their dance steps. Read the deep past. See what you can make of that. That's the way to be original.

title: UNH, Keene, Plymouth offer free tuition to NH families earning up to $100K - Seacoastonline.com
content: DURHAM — The University System of New Hampshire is rolling out a free tuition program in fall 2027 for all newly enrolled in-state students whose families earn a maximum of $100,000 annually. First-year students and transfer students who previously earned an associate degree through the state’s community college system are eligible for the program to be offered at the University of New Hampshire, Keene State College and Plymouth State University. The new USNH program, New Hampshire Promise, will launch ahead for the 2027-2028 academic year and replace the Granite Guarantee program, which currently offers free tuition to Pell grant-eligible in-state students. “New Hampshire’s public institutions of higher education are a transformative opportunity for students,” USNH Chancellor Cathy Provencher said in a prepared statement Oct. 1. “In launching this new program, all of the university system institutions are working together to make higher education more accessible for more New Hampshire students, enabling them to pursue their dreams right here in the Granite State.” The median household income in New Hampshire is just over $99,000, as last reported by the U.S. Census Bureau. Tania deLuzuriaga, a spokesperson for UNH, said the school projects 29% more incoming UNH students will be eligible for New Hampshire Promise than the existing Granite Guarantee program it is replacing. An average of 900 to 1,000 UNH students enroll via the Granite Guarantee program per year, according to deLuzuriaga. “When President (Elizabeth) Chilton got here a little over two years ago, she wanted to shift our need-based program into something income-based just so it was something more families could take advantage of,” she said. Students enrolling at UNH Manchester and for the university’s online courses will be eligible for the new program, too. The university system will not cap the number of students that can enroll in the New Hampshire Promise program. All admitted students meeting the income and education standards, in addition to a minimum 2.7 grade point average requirement, will be automatically accepted after filing their Free Application for Federal Student Aid (FAFSA). There is no separate application to enroll in New Hampshire Promise when the program takes effect. The free tuition will remain in effect should a future student enroll in another USNH institution, so long as they continue to meet the income and education guidelines. “Awards will be based on an annual review of a student’s FAFSA, academic status, and full-time student status,” USNH says. Created in 2017, the Granite Guarantee program will be phased out in several years. Over 4,000 in-state students within the university system have qualified for the program since its founding. Current Granite Guarantee students cannot join the New Hampshire Promise program, though they will retain their financial assistance for the remainder of their undergraduate studies. In-state tuition at UNH’s flagship Durham campus currently stands at $16,304 per year, excluding room and boarding costs. New Hampshire students pay $15,444 per year at Plymouth State University and $12,348 per year at Keene State College. Before the 2025-2026 school year, in-state tuition rates across the university system were unfrozen for the first time in six years. The tuition aid program announcement comes amid declining undergraduate enrollment at UNH’s Durham and Manchester campuses and in its online student population. Last semester, 11,948 full- and part-time undergraduate students attended UNH, down from 13,631 students in the fall 2016 semester, according to a university dashboard.

title: The TRAIL Network - University of New Hampshire
content: W‌alking around the UNH campus on any given day, you'll find ‌COLSA students conducting research alongside faculty, meeting ‌with career advisors in the St. Martin Career Exploration Office, milking cows in the dairy barn, and studying tree growth in College Woods. Others are thousands of miles from campus — in countries such as Italy, Namibia, and New Zealand — immersing themselves in new cultures through experiential learning opportunities.While experiential learning has long been a defining part of the COLSA student experience, Jesse Stabile Morrell ’99, ’04G, ’13G, associate dean for academic affairs, recognized an opportunity to raise awareness of those experiences and help students connect with them more easily.To address that challenge, COLSA launched the TRAIL Network last fall. The TRAIL Network serves as the college's centralized hub for experiential learning opportunities. TRAIL stands for training, research, adventure, internships, and experiential learning. Through the network, every student can chart a personalized path through meaningful experiences that build skills, confidence, and professional connections.The impact of these beyond-the-classroom experiences the college is known for is clear: According to the 2025 First Destination Survey, 93% of COLSA graduates reported being employed or continuing their education."Ultimately, the goal of the TRAIL Network is to help COLSA students get the most out of experiential learning opportunities so they graduate ready for whatever comes next," says Stabile Morrell.As the network continues to grow, it aims to ensure every COLSA student can access the experiences that help turn their passions into career readiness. For students interested in sustainability, UNH is a great university for many reasons. One of the best: the Changemaker Fellowship, a sustainability program open to all first-year students, regardless of major.The Changemaker Fellowship is a program tailored to first-year students who want to turn their passion into action. By participating in the fellowship, students gain valuable leadership skills, build a supportive network of like-minded peers, and develop the tools and confidence needed to turn their ideas into reality.Fellows are paired with a Changemaker Coach, a UNH student with experience in the program. Fellows also participate in monthly workshops and training sessions, plan and participate in community service, and build connections and skills.After students are admitted to UNH, they receive an email from the admissions department inviting them to apply. Have a sustainability-minded young person in your life? title: How 'bout them apples? - University of New Hampshire
content: W‌hen Doug Morin and Emily Meacham set out to purchase an ‌apple orchard in northern New Hampshire or Vermont, there ‌were no established orchards for sale. So, in 2019, they jumped at the chance to acquire a former beef and dairy farm in Whitefield, New Hampshire, to fulfill their goal.Now owners of a property much larger and in need of more work than they originally envisioned, Morin, a wildlife biologist, and Meacham, a forester, wasted no time reaching out to UNH Cooperative Extension. Soon, they were walking the property with Heather Bryant, one of Extension’s fruit and vegetable production field specialists.“Heather was the first person we talked through our ideas with,” Meacham says. “She was the first person to give us confidence to go forward.”They planted their first batch of trees — 500 of them — in 2021, and then the challenges came: drought, wind damage, mole and vole pressure, learning the nuances of integrated pest management, and a fungus that threatened the entire orchard. But they were able to navigate their way through it all with expert — and sometimes extensive — help from Extension.Solving the fungus problem, for example, involved Will Hastings, a fruit and vegetable production specialist in Coös County, staff in UNH’s Plant Diagnostics Lab, Jeremy DeLisle, another fruit and vegetable field production specialist, and Renuka Mathur, a soil health specialist. Thanks to their all-hands-on-deck approach, the trees were saved.“That was a game changer for us,” Meacham says.Now Tellman Hill Farm is producing fruit — primarily apples but also pears — from more than 1,400 trees. Meacham and Morin are looking forward to finally welcoming guests to their own farmstand and orchard this year, a delicious reward after years of hard work and determination and more than a little guidance from Extension specialists.“It’s been amazing to have the support of UNH and folks that say, ‘Here’s what we can do for you,’ or ‘What do you need?’” Morin says. title: Water Watchers - University of New Hampshire
content: W‌akondah Pond in Moultonborough, ‌ringed by forested hills, lay quiet on a ‌summer day last year when Jocelyn Brierley ’26 joined a handful of students and scientists from UNH to gather water samples. Brierley, a zoology major, took the Nalgene bottles full of pond water and packed them on ice for the trip back to Durham, where she was working as a summer intern with the Lakes Lay Monitoring Program (LLMP). The internship offered what she called a “full circle” experience of collecting samples in the field and analyzing them in a laboratory. The researchers, students, and volunteers involved in the LLMP, which dates to 1978, know that a placid surface can conceal troubled waters. Perhaps most troubling is the threat of cyanobacteria, often called blue-green algae. Cyanobacteria are one of the oldest life forms on Earth and occur naturally in water bodies, but that doesn’t make them harmless. In large blooms, some cyanobacteria release a chemical that is toxic to humans and many animals, including dogs. The blooms are sometimes also unsightly, covering a lake or pond’s surface with a thick greenish layer. That’s partly what brought the crew of UNH students and faculty to Wakondah Pond. The pond hadn’t had a problem with cyanobacteria, but Lake Kanasatka, the water body it flows into, had been plagued in recent years until residents spearheaded a treatment in 2024 to remove phosphorus, a nutrient thought to spur blooms. Lake Kanasatka flows into Lake Winnipesaukee, the largest lake in the state. In addition to the monitoring work done around the state by the LLMP, a multidisciplinary team of UNH researchers — including Amanda McQuaid ’06, ’09G, ’19G, Extension state specialist and Extension professor in the department of biological sciences who also serves as the LLMP’s director; Anna O’Brien, assistant professor in the department of molecular, cellular, and biomedical sciences; and Anyin Li, associate professor in the UNH College of Engineering and Physical Sciences’ department of chemistry — is developing new research methods, spurred by the NHAES CREATE program, to study the toxins created by cyanobacteria. They hope to learn where the toxins — and the chemicals that result when the toxins degrade — go because of the risks they can pose to human, animal, and environmental health. O’Brien and McQuaid are also studying whether duckweed, an aquatic plant that commonly grows in irrigation ponds, can safely be used as a fertilizer if the pond it grew in has a cyanobacteria problem. Meanwhile, the LLMP continues to collect data on New Hampshire’s watersheds. Wakondah Pond, which was added to the program in 2021, has been shown to have pristine surface water clarity according to McQuaid, though a common cyanobacterium, Planktothrix, has been detected in its depths. Clarity, plankton, and chlorophyll and phosphorus levels are among the parameters tracked in Wakondah, which will contribute to a deeper understanding of the rest of the watershed, including Lake Winnipesaukee. The LLMP lab, managed by program coordinator Robert Craycraft, boasts some of the most precise phosphorus detection capabilities in the country, if not the world, McQuaid says, for which she can thank long-term support from UNH Cooperative Extension and benefactors such as the Caswell Foundation. The LLMP has been working to protect New Hampshire’s freshwater for nearly 50 years, and such an impact can be sustained only with continued support. The program is fortunate to have found such support from the Caswell Foundation. The Caswell Foundation has supported the LLMP for decades. Its generosity has established reliable revenue streams for the program, enabling the purchase of new equipment and testing supplies and supporting internship opportunities that provide UNH students with invaluable hands-on experience. This year, the LLMP lab in Spaulding Hall will be renamed to honor the Caswell Foundation in recognition of its longstanding support. The naming will serve as a lasting tribute to the foundation’s legacy and impact on the LLMP. Copyright © 2026 , University of New Hampshire. All rights reserved.

title: Giant pumpkins grow from Durham retirement community project with UNH - Granite Post News
content: Giant pumpkins in Durham, NH, are headed to the Deerfield Fair after a growing project brought together residents of Brookdale Spruce Wood, the University of New Hampshire, families, friends and neighbors. Giant pumpkins in Durham, NH, are headed to the Deerfield Fair after a growing project brought together residents of Brookdale Spruce Wood, the University of New Hampshire, families, friends and neighbors. Residents of the retirement community grew five massive pumpkins with help from UNH plant-breeding expert Christopher Hernandez. Several are approaching 800 pounds, and the largest reached about 1,000 pounds before splitting open. To keep reading—and get local New Hampshire news sent daily to your inbox—sign up for our free newsletter! Inspired by the image, Cross and fellow resident, friend and outdoor partner-in-crime Daniel Reich, 86, began researching how to grow a giant pumpkin of their own. Their efforts led them to Christopher Hernandez, assistant professor of plant breeding at the University of New Hampshire. With his guidance, Cross and Reich laid out and rototilled three pumpkin patches. They then made 10 trips to Coyote Spring Farm in Lee to haul horse manure back to the patches. With Hernandez’s help, they obtained seeds from two prize-winning pumpkins, including one grown in 2018 by Steve Geddes of Boscawen that weighed 2,528 pounds (a US record for six years). On June 5, Cross, Reich and Hernandez planted four pumpkin seedlings – initially grown by UNH students – in each of the three pumpkin patches surrounding Brookdale Spruce Wood. Geddes donated retired paper-mill conveyor-belt squares to serve as sturdy “beds” for the pumpkins. He and Hernandez also taught the team about support and cushioning, including the use of sand and pool noodles. Old sheets provided shade and protection from the sun. Cross and Reich tended the plants every day and with Hernandez’s guidance, the team narrowed the field to the two strongest plants in each patch and carefully assisted with pollination. Over the next 16 weeks, throughout July, August and September, the once-tiny seeds/seedlings grew rapidly. The project soon attracted attention beyond Brookdale Spruce Wood. Members of the New Hampshire Giant Pumpkin Association paid the community a visit. Neighbors from the surrounding community stopped by during their daily walks to check on the pumpkins, while visiting family and friends did the same. Those regular visits sparked conversations and new friendships. The largest pumpkin, affectionately named “Frankenstein,” reached an impressive 1,000 pounds before splitting open! Despite the major disappointment, the project continued. Brookdale Spruce Wood residents helped name the four remaining pumpkins: The winning pumpkin will be sent to the Deerfield Fair to compete on Thursday, Oct. 1 against approximately 30 other pumpkins in the heaviest giant-pumpkin and/or prettiest giant-pumpkin competition. title: UNH student organizations celebrate Hispanic Heritage Month with campus-wide events - The Charger Bulletin
content: Hispanic Heritage Month is underway, and student organizations across campus are preparing cultural, artistic and community-centered events. From silent discos to animation displays, resident student organizations (RSOs) are highlighting Hispanic culture, honoring community traditions and bringing students together. The Myatt Center for Diversity and Inclusion anchors the programming each year, but this fall, student-led organizations are taking an especially active role. The Latin American Student Association (LASA), the university’s Animation Club and Greek-letter organizations are collaborating to create one of the most event-packed calendars the university has seen in recent years. A LASA official said that Hispanic Heritage Month is more than a celebration; it is about unity, identity and honoring people who shape Hispanic culture. In a statement given by LASA president Nikki Rosario, a senior marine biology student, and vice president Steven Ojeda, a junior psychology student with a focus in forensics, said: “Hispanic Heritage Month is not just about celebrating one culture but about celebrating our different identities while recognizing what brings us together. We want our members and everyone who attends our events to feel seen, understood, and proud to be part of such a beautiful culture,” they said. “El Apagon represents what LASA is about: Bringing people together through culture and community.” The students said “El Apagon” is one of their favorite events this year, inspired by Bad Bunny’s song and the blackout scene in the 2021 movie, “In the Heights.” Both references use darkness as a symbol of community resilience, something LASA members say they hope to bring to campus. The Animation Club will co-host LA Animación de Cultura with LASA on Oct. 6, focusing on Hispanic representation in animation. Animation Club president Gian Rodriguez, a senior graphic & digital design student, shared why this event matters. “As a Mexican and Puerto Rican student, it is amazing to see fellow Hispanic animators mold and shape what Hispanic culture is in animation,” he said. The event will explore both positive representation and harmful stereotypes in animated media. Students will also have the chance to create their own character inspired by Hispanic Culture. “We feel it is important to showcase and talk about the involvement of culturally rich communities in animation, as they are part of the beauty that helps make such captivating pieces of media,” Rodriguez said. Students will have opportunities to engage with art, music, film, dance and cultural education all led by organizations committed to uplifting Hispanic voices. From LASA’s community-centered programming to the Animation Club’s creative showcase, this year’s Hispanic Heritage Month events highlight the diversity, resilience and joy of Hispanic culture at the university. title: Food Among the Trees - University of New Hampshire
content: ‌New Hampshire is more than 80% forested, second ‌in coverage only to Maine in the U.S. The Adaptive ‌Agroforestry Principles and Teaching (ADAPT) program is leveraging this important resource through the testing and teaching of agroforestry concepts and methods, work that will support local farming and sustain a stronger regional food system. Agroforestry expands agricultural opportunities by embracing, rather than seeking to overcome, the tree-filled landscape. ADAPT is a collaborative effort led by Heidi Asbjornsen, professor of natural resources and the environment, that also includes researchers at Yale University, Dartmouth College, and 12 operating farms. ADAPT works with three primary types of agroforestry. Forest farming grows shade-tolerant crops under an existing tree canopy. Food forests contain food-producing plants of varying heights, such as nut trees, berry bushes, and herbs, within the same space. And silvopasture provides livestock pasturing and grazing space among trees. Unlike most fully cleared pasture and crop lands, all offer welcoming habitats for beneficial insects, pollinators, and wildlife. “Agroforestry can increase crop diversity and sustainability, providing farmers and growers with more resilience in changing conditions as well as expanding income-generating opportunities,” says Asbjornsen. “But agroforestry systems are complex to manage. Education and extension are critical parts of ADAPT so that we can share our research-based insights with the community.” Copyright © 2026 , University of New Hampshire. All rights reserved.

title: Chipotle Opens Near UNH in Durham, New Hampshire - Hoodline
content: Chipotle Mexican Grill is planting a new flag steps from the University of New Hampshire campus, with a restaurant planned at 7 Mill Road, Suite A, in Durham on Sept. 29, 2026. It follows an Aug. 19 opening in Braintree, Massachusetts, marking a fresh push by the burrito chain into the Boston-Manchester corridor. The Durham location sits near the UNH campus, according to Boston Real Estate Times. The Braintree restaurant, at 165 Pearl St., opened Aug. 19, giving Chipotle two fresh footholds in the region within about six weeks of each other. UNH provides a substantial nearby campus backdrop, though its degree-seeking enrollment in Durham dipped from 13,360 in fall 2024 to 12,819 in fall 2025. The university also said it received 2,471 first-year deposits for fall 2026, nearly 4% more than a year earlier. The figures offer a snapshot of the student population close to the new restaurant, without indicating how many students will become customers. UNH’s Durham enrollment history and fall 2026 admissions update provide the counts. The Durham address falls within Durham Landing, a retail property marketed by Eastern Retail as having 10,700 square feet of existing endcap space and redeveloped small-shop units ranging from 1,730 to 7,885 square feet, subdividable to fit different tenants. Eastern Retail's listing describes the property as ideal for full-service and quick-service restaurants, along with fitness and medical uses, suggesting Chipotle is one of several types of businesses the site was built to attract. Durham's own planning records point to a larger redevelopment underway in the same area. A site-plan page on the town's website identifies a Mill Plaza project at 5 Mill Road involving architectural improvements to the building facade and other exterior renovations, with 5-7 Mill Road LLC listed as the property owner. A separate site-plan review application on file with the town references 7 Mill Road, Unit L, as part of that broader Mill Plaza redevelopment, which the filing describes as including 108 residential units, 258 beds, and roughly 80,250 square feet of total commercial space once complete. The Mill Plaza property has a longer planning history distinct from the current restaurant opening. In 2022, Durham’s Planning Board denied a redevelopment application for Mill Plaza, and the state Housing Appeals Board affirmed that decision later that year. Town records identify 5 and 7 Mill Road as being in Durham’s Central Business zoning district. That history puts the new storefront within a site that has previously drawn formal land-use review, but does not establish that Chipotle’s tenancy was part of the earlier proposal. The town’s account of the 2022 denial and its update on the appeal document those decisions. Both the Braintree and Durham restaurants are expected to create employment opportunities in the region, and Chipotle is hiring for both, with each location carrying approximately 30 open positions, per the same report. Once open, both restaurants are set to run daily from 10:45 a.m. to 10 p.m., the outlet reports. The expansion adds to Chipotle's presence in the broader Boston and New Hampshire markets, as the chain continues building out its footprint across the region. The two local openings also come amid a wider company expansion. Chipotle ended 2025 with 4,056 restaurants and opened 334 company-owned locations that year, while comparable restaurant sales fell 1.7%. The company forecast 350 to 370 new openings in 2026. The figures place the Braintree and Durham restaurants within a national growth push, even as the chain reported a year-over-year decline in sales at established locations. Chipotle’s 2025 results and 2026 outlook give the companywide totals. Chipotle is also promoting new and limited-time menu offerings across the Boston-Manchester region, including pollo asado, a grilled chicken option seasoned with garlic and Mexican spices and finished with cilantro and citrus, alongside chili lime chips seasoned with lime and chili peppers. The chain is pairing that with a high-protein menu for the market, featuring items ranging from 15 to 81 grams of protein, such as a double high-protein bowl, a high protein-high fiber bowl, and a high-protein cup, plus a single chicken taco starting at $3.50. Chipotle Rewards members can also tap into monthly food rewards and customizable birthday benefits, while new members can receive free chips and guac with a purchase. The chain additionally offers family meal options built for groups eating at home, and local organizations can use Chipotle's fundraising program, which helps groups raise money for community causes through restaurant-based fundraising events. For the roughly 60 workers Chipotle hopes to hire across the two new restaurants, the company points to a broader benefits package. Employees are eligible for a crew bonus program that can provide the chance to earn an additional month's pay each year, along with a debt-free college degree program. Workers also have access to English-as-a-second-language support, and employees and their families can access mental health care, according to the same report. title: Counting the Recovery of New Hampshire Bats - University of New Hampshire
content: New Hampshire bats have been in crisis for years. Beginning in 2009, a fatal fungal disease known as white-nose syndrome devastated all five of the state’s cave-hibernating bat species. Researchers and Extension specialists in COLSA are now teaming up with the NH Fish and Game Department and Granite State landowners to support one of the state’s key programs supporting the conservation and recovery of the remaining bat populations: NH Bat Counts. Laura Kloepper, associate professor of biological sciences, leads UNH’s Ecological Acoustics and Behavior Lab, studying how animals use acoustics to navigate the world and how we, in turn, can use acoustics to monitor them. Acoustic technology has gotten both better and less expensive in recent years, and it can now be applied to NH Bat Counts. “NH Bat Counts has been active for a long time, and we’re joining it now to contribute our experience with advanced technology to expand and improve data gathering,” says Kloepper. “The work is vital for tracking bat abundance and providing insights to protect them and their habitats.” Why do bats matter to us? Estimates vary, but studies indicate bats contribute at least $3.7 billion and potentially more than $50 billion in insect pest control for U.S. agriculture alone every year. Without them, controlling pests becomes more costly and losses for New Hampshire industries such as agriculture and forestry increase. White-nose syndrome was first detected in hibernating bats in New York State in 2006. When it arrived in New Hampshire in 2009, surveys of the four largest caves and mines favored by bats for hibernation counted 3,230 of these flying mammals. By 2011, that number had plummeted to 16. For reasons that remain poorly understood, some species of bats elsewhere have proven to be more resilient to the fungus that causes white-nose syndrome. And some colonies are beginning to grow once again, though their numbers remain much smaller than pre-disease. “There has been growth in some of the maternity colonies over the last few years,” says Haley Andreozzi ’13G, Extension state specialist and Extension professor of wildlife conservation. “In 2022, we had a colony with more than 700 individuals, the first time we’ve measured one that large. There’s a long way to go — pre-disease, some colonies had thousands of bats — but we’re beginning to see some small but needed wins for the bats.” The NH Fish and Game Department, NH Audubon, and U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service launched NH Bat Counts in 2012 to find and quantify the survivors. The program monitors summer bat colonies in barns, attics, steeples, and other structures where female bats gather and give birth to their young during the warmer months. NH Bat Counts is now spearheaded by Sandra Houghton ’04G, wildlife diversity biologist with the NH Fish and Game Department, and Andreozzi. Houghton and Andreozzi have worked together to extend and formalize the program over the past half dozen years. “The data from NH Bat Counts volunteers furthers our knowledge about the location, species, and status of bat colonies in New Hampshire,” says Houghton. “It helps us prioritize conservation efforts while also creating a network of bat ambassadors.” Kloepper’s work will make it possible to look at trends in the acoustic energy produced by the bats to get a sense of movement within the colonies, the timing of pup independence, how environmental conditions such as weather impact pup emergence and roost shifting, and more. The recorders will also allow volunteers to obtain nightly population estimates far more efficiently than previously possible. Andreozzi notes the interest and enthusiasm of the volunteers, who enjoy learning about how valuable their barns and other structures are for bats and contributing to the efforts to protect bat colonies. Now, Kloepper’s expertise and recorder technologies will enable the volunteers to help even more. She has also involved her students in the research and outreach efforts, and eight undergraduates have formed a “bat count” team devoted to devising better ways to count bats for conservation. “It’s a great example of how research is being done at UNH,” says Kloepper. “All parties — researchers, students, Extension, and state experts — are out in the New Hampshire community, working together toward a common goal.” Copyright © 2026 , University of New Hampshire. title: What Are UNH Stock Investors Betting On? - Trefis
content: UnitedHealth (UNH) stock trades at 22.5 times its past year’s adjusted earnings, which are normalized net income with stock-based pay added back. That multiple leaves little room for error after three years of shrinking operating margins, sitting near the stock’s 10-year median despite fundamentally weaker profitability. But the price looks different against the profit expected for fiscal 2026 and fiscal 2027. So what are UnitedHealth investors betting on? UnitedHealth investors are betting on wider margins in fiscal 2026 and fiscal 2027. A P/E is the share price divided by a year of profit. On the consensus forecast for fiscal 2026, today’s price is 19.0 times earnings. On the fiscal 2027 forecast, it is 16.8 times, beside 22.5 times for the past year. The consensus forecast has profit rising 12.9% from fiscal 2026 to fiscal 2027. Sales in the forecast rise just 3.0% over the same year. Profit only outgrows sales when a company keeps more of each dollar of sales. So the forecast P/Es are real only if UnitedHealth’s net margin widens—an expansion that ultimately depends on reversing the slide in its operating margins. Not over the last three years. Operating margin is the share of sales left after medical and running costs. At UnitedHealth, it fell each year, from 8.8% three years ago to 4.8% now. UnitedHealth’s margins did widen in the second quarter of fiscal 2026. Operating earnings grew 55% from a year earlier on flat revenue. Management credited product and portfolio changes, and said better results in Medicare Advantage put its UnitedHealthcare business ahead of expectations. Medical costs that quarter were also flattered by $860 million in favorable reserve adjustments—mostly developed from earlier in 2026—giving a substantial one-time boost to that 55% operating jump. Management then raised its fiscal 2026 guidance for adjusted earnings per share to $19.50 to $20. The consensus forecast of $19.95 per share for fiscal 2026 is near the top of that guidance. Management called that range the right baseline to build toward its long-term earnings growth goal of 13% to 16%. The forecast’s fiscal 2027 profit growth is at about the low end of that goal. If those costs do not ease, the consensus forecast for fiscal 2027 profit is more likely to fall than rise. Medicare Advantage is the other major risk, despite driving the second quarter’s beat. Management said its own changes to benefits, care management and networks were a primary reason Medicare costs grew less than expected. Then, over three days, she scored her first two collegiate goals in a 4-1 win over Northeastern, followed by another goal in a 4-2 win over Merrimack. (Photo by Alex Miller) “Ava has been a very positive story for us,” said Welham. “She has developed each year and is taking this opportunity and really running with it. She can fly – she has a great engine, great endurance, and she’s just really coming into her own.” The rehabilitation process was hardly sunshine and rainbows for VanBuskirk. “It was hard mentally. I had never been a player who was on the sidelines to watch. That was a big transition going from always playing and soccer always being my outlet, and then not having that,” said VanBuskirk, an aspiring elementary school teacher. “My teammates were awesome and always included me. It was about finding my role on the team in a different way. … I took the role of being on the bench and cheering as loud as I could.” VanBuskirk went to physical therapy three times a week and worked with different trainers to regain her strength and mobility. Those grueling workouts are now paying off. She’s been electric on the field, said Welham. “She’s two-footed. She loves to go 1-versus-1 on a defender,” he said. “She’s technical, she’s dynamic, and her game is built around pace and dynamic movement on and off the ball. Her energy and positivity coming off the bench have just elevated the team to another level.” Ava VanBuskirk during her time in Marlborough (Photo/Jesse Kucewicz) Her first collegiate goal – a rebound off an initial shot taken by Elizabeth Finn – was “such a surreal feeling,” she said. At the time of the score, VanBuskirk was focused on getting back on the field; scoring was simply an added bonus. “I was really focusing on coming back from my injury and trying to get back to where I was before, so when I got my opportunity to get on the field and play, I took it and did my best,” VanBuskirk said. “Instead of stressing myself out, I focused on having fun and why I play the sport. It really helped that the girls around me supported me and were excited for me, along with my family, friends, and coaches.” Thirteen minutes after her first collegiate goal, VanBuskirk scored another. Each time, her “large soccer family” – including her mother Pam, a Marlborough soccer alum; her brother Joey; and her aunt, uncle, and cousin, who all played collegiately – were there to celebrate in the stands. Ava VanBuskirk during her time in Marlborough (Photo/Jesse Kucewicz) “Soccer has always been a part of my life,” VanBuskirk said. “I looked up to my brother and older cousins, and we played soccer on every family outing and summer trip, always with a soccer ball. It was nice being able to grow up with everyone, especially my brother, because he’s always been my biggest role model, and I always wanted to make him proud.” Unlock the power of local outreach with our platform! title: Giant pumpkins grow from Durham retirement community project with UNH - Foster's Daily Democrat
content: DURHAM — Giant pumpkins were grown by residents of Brookdale Spruce Wood, a retirement community, and one will be entered in the Deerfield Fair. The community project brought together people from Brookdale Spruce Wood, the University of New Hampshire, families, friends and neighbors, resulting in five very big pumpkins. The Brookdale Spruce Wood UNH giant pumpkin project began in 2025, when a photograph of an enormous pumpkin caught residents' attention during a presentation about “Our Backyard” by resident Jim Cross, 79, an outdoor enthusiast and nature lover. Inspired by the image, Cross and fellow resident, friend and outdoor partner-in-crime Daniel Reich, 86, began researching how to grow a giant pumpkin of their own. Their efforts led them to Christopher Hernandez, assistant professor of plant breeding at the University of New Hampshire. With his guidance, Cross and Reich laid out and rototilled three pumpkin patches. They then made 10 trips to Coyote Spring Farm in Lee to haul horse manure back to the patches. With Hernandez's help, they obtained seeds from two prize-winning pumpkins, including one grown in 2018 by Steve Geddes of Boscawen that weighed 2,528 pounds (a U.S. record for six years). On June 5, Cross, Reich and Hernandez planted four pumpkin seedlings – initially grown by UNH students – in each of the three pumpkin patches surrounding Brookdale Spruce Wood. Geddes donated retired paper-mill conveyor-belt squares to serve as sturdy “beds” for the pumpkins. He and Hernandez also taught the team about support and cushioning, including the use of sand and pool noodles. Old sheets provided shade and protection from the sun. Cross and Reich tended the plants every day and with Hernandez's guidance, the team narrowed the field to the two strongest plants in each patch and carefully assisted with pollination. Over the next 16 weeks, throughout July, August and September, the once-tiny seeds/seedlings grew rapidly. The project soon attracted attention beyond Brookdale Spruce Wood. Members of the New Hampshire Giant Pumpkin Association paid the community a visit. Neighbors from the surrounding community stopped by during their daily walks to check on the pumpkins, while visiting family and friends did the same. Those regular visits sparked conversations and new friendships. The largest pumpkin, affectionately named “Frankenstein,” reached an impressive 1,000 pounds before splitting open! Despite the major disappointment, the project continued. Brookdale Spruce Wood residents helped name the four remaining pumpkins: The group plans to officially weigh the pumpkins on Wednesday, Sept. 30. The winning pumpkin will be sent to the Deerfield Fair to compete on Thursday, Oct. 1 against approximately 30 other pumpkins in the heaviest giant-pumpkin and/or prettiest giant-pumpkin competition.

title: Mel Rines ’47 Makes $1M Gift to Bolster Key Priority in UNH Strategic Plan - University of New Hampshire
content: Mel Rines ’47 (seated) recently made a $1M gift to UNH. Mel Rines ’47 recently made his largest one-time gift ever to UNH, a $1 million contribution that will impact students from a wide swath of disciplines and academic areas while advancing a key pillar of President Elizabeth Chilton’s strategic plan for the university. Rines – who is among the university’s most generous benefactors – recently made the gift to bolster Chilton’s focus on interdisciplinary education and research excellence, support that will help advance one of four strategic priorities in Chilton’s “One UNH: Roadmap to 2030” initiative and is also a seamless match for Rines’ personal philosophy. “Be bold, aim high, and have fun” is a favorite motto of Rines, who graduated from UNH as a psychology major and U.S. Naval fighter pilot before ultimately spending his career in the investment business. He had lofty goals from the start, with a desire for independence and helping mankind, and was guided by a personal mantra – “success on my terms.” So, it’s only fitting that his latest gift lands at the intersection of flexibility and innovation at UNH. It is the largest contribution to UNH for Rines, who has donated steadily since his initial support in 1982, extending a deep relationship with the university that began during his days as a student. Rines’ tenure at UNH was interrupted when he joined the Navy and trained as a fighter pilot during World War II. After graduating from UNH, he went on to study optometry and joined a Naval reserve fighter squadron. That squadron was the first to be recalled at the start of the Korean War in 1950 where he flew the first jets in active combat off the aircraft carrier USS Boxer. His years traveling and meeting others as a U.S. Navy fighter pilot broadened his thinking about career opportunities. Leaving the Navy, Rines passed on an opportunity to pilot commercial airplanes, embarking instead on a new challenge, a career in the investment world. Rines, now 102, went on to carve out a successful and fulfilling 46-year career beginning as a retail broker, culminating in international investment banking with the firm that first employed him, Kidder Peabody. He worked closely with the development banks and the International Monetary Fund to help developing nations access international credit markets to help fuel their infrastructure projects and economic development. Rines first reconnected with UNH in 1982 by seeding and co-directing the International Private Enterprise Center at the Whittemore School of Business and Economics, now Paul College. “UNH has always been dear to me,” Rines says. “I’ve always been so fond of the professors and the students.” Rines’ previous giving also focused on university-wide opportunities. His gifts led to the creation of offerings like the Rines Student Angel Investment Fund and the International Changemakers Grant (formally Student International Service Initiative) – programs that encourage involvement from students from all majors. “My father wanted to create innovative programs that would go across departments of the university,” his daughter, Marcy Venezia, says. “You see that with the Rines Angel Fund where you don’t have to be a business major to become a part of it.” Indeed, the Rines Angel Fund – a hands-on program that immerses students in the realm of early-stage investing – is housed within the Peter T. Paul College of Business and Economics, but participation is encouraged across all majors. Similarly, the International Changemaker Grant, which allows students to travel globally and work on sustainability projects that establish relationships with international communities of need, is open to UNH students from any college. The Rines Angel Fund gives students real-world experience within the angel fund ecosystem and the International Changemaker Grant gives them a chance to contribute to significant sustainability work while traveling to areas of the world they may not otherwise get to see. David Rines, Mel’s son, says one of the goals of the changemaker grant was “for students who might not have left New Hampshire before to have an opportunity to do something really meaningful outside the US.” “I think both the Rines Angel Fund and the International Changemaker Grant are about giving students real-world experience outside the classroom that make a real difference in terms of their career opportunities. It’s so gratifying to feel like these students have opportunities that I didn’t see growing up,” says David Rines. Adds Venezia, “It was that emphasis on moving away from just straight academics into real-world experience that always resonated with my father.” Rines’ focus through it all has been to create as many opportunities as possible for UNH students. He and his family have been able to witness up-close how much of an impact the Rines Angel Fund and International Changemaker Grant have had in terms of opening real-world career opportunities to students. So, it’s no wonder Rines became immediately intrigued after hearing about President Chilton’s Roadmap to 2030 priorities. In November of 2025, The Rines family hosted Chilton and learned more about her vision, a meeting that ultimately inspired the $1 million commitment to advance the interdisciplinary education and research effort. “It was gratifying to hear about all the work that was already underway on the Roadmap and this gift felt like something that would further support President Chilton and her initiatives while also being in line with my father’s interest in innovation and interdisciplinary learning,” says David Rines. “We’re excited to see where this can go.” Rines’ UNH affection runs deep. He has been a dedicated volunteer at UNH for more than two decades, is a former chair of the UNH Foundation Board, and currently serves on the emeriti board, the Rines Student Angel Investment Fund investment committee, and the International Changemakers Grant committee. Beyond The Rines Angel Fund and the International Changemaker Grant, Rines’ generosity has led to the establishment of several additional funds, including the S. Melvin and Mary Jo Rines Art Exhibit Fund and the Mel Rines ’47 Fellowship Fund. Mel and his wife, Mary Jo Rines, were honored in 2007 with UNH’s Hubbard Family Award for Service to Philanthropy, the highest honor bestowed upon those whose philanthropic leadership has strengthened the state, its communities, and the university. Through all of that, David Rines and his sister have long witnessed their father’s commitment to both people-centered philanthropy and his alma mater. His legacy at UNH was cemented long before this most recent gift, but the contribution to interdisciplinary education and research excellence is yet another illustration of that combination that will carry forward for years to come. Venezia says, “My father is not one to say, ‘I did that.’ He’s not a showman in that way. He always quietly encourages the people around him, and he’s done that with us, and he’s doing that now with his ideas about philanthropy.” Copyright © 2026 , University of New Hampshire. title: USNH Launches New Free Tuition Program for N.H. Families Making Up to $100K - University of New Hampshire
content: A UNH education is now within reach for more New Hampshire families, thanks to the New Hampshire Promise, a new program launched by the University System of New Hampshire. Beginning in fall 2027, incoming first-year and transfer students from families earning up to $100,000 a year can have their tuition covered at any USNH institution, removing a major financial barrier and giving more students the opportunity to pursue their goals and build their future in New Hampshire. “New Hampshire’s public institutions of higher education are a transformative opportunity for students,” USNH Chancellor Cathy Provencher says. “In launching this new program, all of the university system institutions are working together to make higher education more accessible for more New Hampshire students, enabling them to pursue their dreams right here in the Granite State.” Under the terms of the program, New Hampshire residents who are admitted as full-time, first-year students or transfers who have graduated from a New Hampshire community college, with total family income of up to $100,000, qualify to attend a USNH institution — UNH Durham, UNH Manchester, UNH College of Professional Studies Online, Plymouth State University, and Keene State College — tuition-free. With New Hampshire’s median household income of $99,782, according to recent U.S. Census Bureau data, the program has the potential to benefit a significant portion of the state’s families. “The New Hampshire Promise program is an investment in our students and in the future of our state. By expanding affordable pathways to higher education, we’re creating more opportunities for our young people to pursue good-paying jobs and making it easier for them to build their careers in New Hampshire," says New Hampshire Gov. Kelly Ayotte. "I thank the University System of New Hampshire for their efforts to make college more affordable for New Hampshire students and their families.” Admitted students who submit a Free Application for Federal Student Aid (FAFSA) will automatically be considered for the New Hampshire Promise; there is no separate application process. While the program covers tuition, it does not cover housing, food, books, or fees. The New Hampshire Promise replaces USNH’s Granite Guarantee program, established in 2017 to provide free tuition to Pell-eligible New Hampshire students. Since its inception, more than 4,000 students have qualified for this program. Currently enrolled USNH undergraduates will remain in Granite Guarantee to ensure no disruption of financial aid benefits. The program is the latest effort to make college more affordable in the Granite State. Last month, the University of New Hampshire announced that it awarded a record $40 million in financial aid to incoming students this year, with the average student award topping $16,000. Almost every student in the incoming class (96%) received financial aid, with an average award of $16,918, an increase of more than 50% from the prior year. These efforts, combined with UNH’s high student success rates, led to UNH being named New England’s No. 1 best value public university for the sixth consecutive year, according to the Best Value Schools rankings of National Universities by U.S. News & World Report. According to UNH’s most recent graduating class survey data, UNH graduates boast a 94% success rate, with 71.6% of students employed within 12 months after graduation and another 22.2% enrolled in further education. Additionally, the significant majority of employed graduates — 88% — reported that their job was directly or somewhat related to their major. Copyright © 2026 , University of New Hampshire. title: Before and After: Rare Opportunities to Study Stream Water Quality - University of New Hampshire
content: New Hampshire’s 19,000 miles of rivers and streams, from the Connecticut River in the west to the waters flowing to the Atlantic Ocean in the east, shape the state’s lives, livelihoods, and landscapes. New Hampshire Agricultural Experiment Station researchers at the University of New Hampshire are measuring how water characteristics and quality, both in and along rivers and estuaries, are directly affected by man- and nature-made changes to surrounding landscapes and infrastructure. The team is taking advantage of three rare opportunities to study rivers and streams before and after significant changes to better understand how New Hampshire’s communities along a river’s path could be impacted by changes in water quality, as well as the effects on greenhouse gas emissions and nitrogen quantities. “It’s unusual to be able to measure streams before and after significant restoration events,” says Station scientist Wilfred Wollheim, the Josephine A. Lamprey Professor in Climate and Sustainability and professor in the UNH department of natural resources and the environment. “The data we’re collecting before and after human-made dam removal, beaver dam construction, and our own restoration project will provide insights that are relevant throughout New Hampshire.” Wollheim, who also co-directs the Water Systems Analysis Group, is leading the studies. The research focuses on comparing water quality before and after the removal of the Mill Pond Dam in Durham, understanding the impacts of restoring a currently buried stretch of College Brook on the UNH campus, and measuring the effects of a new beaver dam built at a formerly flowing stream site that has been monitored for a quarter century. While the expectation is that each change will help improve water quality, alter greenhouse gas emissions, and reduce the amount of nitrogen flowing downstream, the goal of each study is to test that hypothesis and quantify the size of those impacts. Many years ago, College Brook wound its way through the UNH campus. As the University campus expanded, the brook was culverted underground to accommodate new Student Recreation Fields. However, this diversion limited natural processes, including rapidly flushing water and materials such as nitrate, road salt, and sediment through the system. Wollheim and Jojo Baldus, an ecosystem science graduate student in the Wollheim lab, are measuring pre-restoration water quality now and how it is affected by heavy rainfall in storms. Plans for the restoration itself have been prepared and once funded, the project will restore the stream above ground, allow streamside vegetation to regrow, and establish a streamside wetland to absorb storm water. “We know that storms are especially interesting ‘hot moments,’ when rainfall and runoff can quickly transport materials from the landscape into streams like College Brook,” says Baldus. “Once restored, College Brook will be able to more effectively capture, transform, and store some of these materials in the streambed and surrounding soils and vegetation, helping to improve water quality and ecosystem health in the brook and in Great Bay.” Beavers did much of the work for Wollheim and his team on a stream at the Plum Island Ecological Research site just south of the New Hampshire state line on the coast of Massachusetts. The researchers had been monitoring water quality in the stream for about 25 years before the beavers assembled a dam just downstream from the research location. The fortuitous change will allow Wollheim and Kylie Short, a student whose work is supported by the National Science Foundation’s Research Experiences for Undergraduates program, to measure exactly how beaver ponds change water quality and greenhouse gas emissions over time. “The creation of beaver ponds can dramatically transform the landscape and influence methane production in the pond,” says Short. “Trees die and are eventually replaced by aquatic plants, changing the gas dynamics and establishing a new ecosystem. We can now study the process in real time and compare the stream before and after the dam was established.” Additional recent support from the National Science Foundation to expand this work will involve combining remote sensing, artificial intelligence, and other tools to map and characterize beaver-created ecosystems in the Northeast. Working with researchers at the University of Connecticut and Cornell University, the goal is an online mapping tool to aid local decision-makers in land management efforts. The removal of the human-made Mill Pond dam on the Oyster River in Durham provides a different before-and-after scenario. Few of New England’s estimated 14,000 dams are still used to generate power, and while data about what happens when a dam is removed is scarce, findings at other sites, such as along the Penobscot River in Maine, suggest benefits for both fish habitats and streambed and wetland environments. In Durham, researchers are measuring water quality in and around Mill Pond, including during storms, so that they can compare it post-removal and better understand how human-led landscape and river management decisions affect river characteristics. The College Brook and Oyster River changes have implications that go beyond their streambeds and nearby environments. Both drain into Great Bay, a coastal estuary that plays a variety of important economic and ecosystem services roles in New Hampshire’s coastal ecosystem, such as harboring fish during their journey from stream to ocean and being the hub for New Hampshire’s oyster aquaculture industry. Lately, freshwater quality issues may have contributed to some concerning changes in Great Bay. “The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency has classified Great Bay as nitrogen impaired, a condition in which more algae can grow and limit native plants like eelgrass,” says Wollheim. “It’s not in a good state at the moment, and its future health could be in serious jeopardy.” The issue underscores the fact that stream health and water quality affect all parts of New Hampshire, from the mountainous inland to the busy coast. Can the latest research tools and methods help to better understand how natural and planned landscape changes impact New Hampshire’s water quality now and in the future? Wollheim and his lab are working hard to find the answer to that vital question. Copyright © 2026 , University of New Hampshire. All rights reserved.
